paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend. You cannot outrun God, and you don't have to be afraid of what He asks. Jonah gets a clear word from the LORD and heads the opposite way, and the whole trip is about getting as far as he can "away from the presence of the LORD" (Jonah 1:3). But look who sends the wind. "Then the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea" (Jonah 1:4). Wherever Jonah goes, God is already there.

Now watch what happens next, because it's wild. Jonah is asleep below deck while the sailors are crying out to their own gods and the captain has to come wake him up (Jonah 1:5-6). Then Jonah says, "I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land" (Jonah 1:9). Friend, that's a man who knows exactly who God is and still ran. Knowing the right answer and doing the right thing are two different cookies, and I've burned a few batches learning that. Jonah does own it, though: "I know that I am to blame for this violent storm that has come upon you" (Jonah 1:12).

And here's the part I want you to carry out of my bakery. When Jonah runs, other people feel the storm too, and yet God is working even in the middle of it. The sailors end up crying out to the LORD, and "the men feared the LORD greatly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows to Him" (Jonah 1:16). So when God asks something hard of you, baker, don't book the ticket to Tarshish. Run toward Him, because running away only takes you somewhere you'll want to come back from. And Jonah's story isn't over yet.
